analysis.one_liner: Makes senior executives at the biggest banks put up part of their pay to cover their banks' misconduct fines.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee: referred to the House Financial Services Committee in July 2019, it received no cosponsors and no hearing or vote before the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would require the very largest banks — those with over $250 billion in assets — to hold back at least half of the pay each senior executive earns above ten times what the bank's median employee makes. That deferred money would sit in a fund for ten years, and if the bank gets hit with a civil or criminal fine for misconduct, the fine comes out of that fund first, before bank profits. Executives get their deferred pay back after ten years only if it wasn't needed for fines. The idea is that the bankers responsible for misconduct, not the bank's ordinary shareholders, should bear the cost of the fines.
analysis.who_benefits: Bank shareholders, who currently absorb billions in fines for executive misconduct — the bill's findings note that DOJ actions against every major bank produced more than $163 billion in fines paid from money that otherwise could have gone to shareholders, while the culpable executives kept their full pay. By extension, ordinary people with 401(k)s and pensions invested in bank stock, and anyone who wants misconduct deterred at the source rather than paid for out of the corporate till.

how_it_helps.text: Each covered bank must defer at least 50% of a senior employee's compensation that exceeds 10 times the median employee's pay, into a fund usable only for paying fines.
If the bank or a subsidiary is fined, civil or criminal, the fine must be paid out of the deferment fund first.
Deferred compensation that cannot be repaid after ten years because fines drained the fund is cancelled, so executives personally lose pay when their misconduct costs the bank.
Former employees' deferred pay is protected from being used to pay fines for misconduct that happened after they left, keeping the penalty tied to the people responsible for the wrongdoing.

analysis.who_pays: Senior executives — the highest-paid officers — at banks with more than $250 billion in assets, whose large bonuses would be held for ten years and cancelled if needed to pay fines, plus the banks themselves, which would face new administration requirements and could see pressure to raise pay or restructure compensation to blunt the rule.

drawbacks.text: The penalty falls on the bank's 100 most senior or best-paid employees collectively, so executives can lose deferred pay for misconduct they had no hand in — the bill mitigates this for ex-employees but not for current ones.

It applies only to bank holding companies above $250 billion in assets, so misconduct at smaller banks and nonbank lenders would go untouched, and large firms could potentially shift pay or risk-taking to affiliates outside the definition.
Mandated ten-year deferrals add administrative complexity, and banks could simply raise senior compensation to offset the value locked up, diluting the deterrent.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea is sound and targeted: it redirects the cost of misconduct fines from innocent shareholders to the executives whose behavior caused them, and it makes deferred pay a real consequence rather than a gesture. The design is imperfect — collective deferral can penalize uninvolved executives, and the scope is limited to the very largest banks — but the drawbacks are modest compared to a straightforward accountability gain. The bill never got a hearing, so there was no chance to refine or test these tradeoffs.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Tulsi Gabbard introduced the bill on July 23, 2019.
It was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services the same day.
The House Financial Services Committee never acted on the bill, and it received no further action before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Senior executives at the largest banks are better off: nothing changed, so misconduct fines are still paid out of bank funds that would otherwise go to shareholders, and top bankers keep their full compensation regardless of their conduct.

for.name: Rep. Tulsi Gabbard
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the House.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (Chair: Rep. Maxine Waters, D-CA)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill — no hearing, markup, or vote — after it was referred on the day of introduction.

sides.party_line_note: There was never a floor vote or recorded position; the bill had a single Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors from either party, so no partisan split ever formed in the record.

industries.industry: Large bank holding companies (over $250 billion in assets)
industries.note: The bill would make these banks pay fines out of executives' deferred compensation rather than corporate funds, and impose deferral and cancellation policies on senior pay. Their interest is in keeping the current arrangement, in which shareholders absorb the fines and executives keep full pay.

industries.industry: Senior bank executives (top-paid officers at megabanks)
industries.note: They would have at least half of pay above ten times the median employee's salary deferred for ten years, forfeited if the bank's misconduct fines drain the fund. Their interest in the bill's defeat runs directly against holding misconduct accountable.

industries.industry: Bank shareholders, including pension and 401(k) investors
industries.note: Fines for executive misconduct would stop being paid from money that otherwise flows to shareholders. This group includes ordinary retirement savers, not just institutions.
